original_value: AbstractCryptocurrencies as a new way of transferring assets and securing financial transactions have gained popularity in recent years. Transactions in cryptocurrencies are publicly available, hence, statistical studies on different aspects of these currencies are possible. However, previous statistical analysis on cryptocurrencies transactions have been very limited and mostly devoted to Bitcoin, with no comprehensive comparison between these currencies. In this study, we intend to compare the transaction graph of Bitcoin, Ethereum, Litecoin, Dash, and Z-Cash, with respect to the dynamics of their transaction graphs over time, and discuss their properties. In particular, we observed that the growth rate of the nodes and edges of the transaction graphs, and the density of these graphs, are closely related to the price of these currencies. We also found that the transaction graph of these currencies is non-assortative, i.e. addresses do not tend for transact with a particular type of addresses of higher or lower degree, and the degree sequence of their transaction graph follows the power law distribution.

result.paraphrase: AbstractCryptocurrencies, as a new means of transferring assets and securing financial transactions, have become increasingly popular in recent years. Because cryptocurrency transactions are publicly available, statistical studies on different aspects of these currencies are possible. However, prior statistical analyses of cryptocurrency transactions have been very limited and focused mostly on Bitcoin, with no comprehensive comparison among these currencies. In this study, we aim to compare the transaction graphs of Bitcoin, Ethereum, Litecoin, Dash, and Z-Cash in terms of how their transaction graphs evolve over time, and to discuss their properties. In particular, we observed that the growth rates of the nodes and edges in the transaction graphs, as well as the density of these graphs, are closely related to the price of these currencies. We also found that the transaction graphs of these currencies are non-assortative, meaning that addresses do not tend to transact with a particular type of address of higher or lower degree, and that the degree sequence of their transaction graphs follows a power law distribution.
